analysis.title: US Midterms: The Market Playbook, The Risks and The Races
key_insights: UBS Evidence Lab puts the implied probability of Democratic control at 97% in the House (7% Republican) and 81% in the Senate (25% Republican). RealClearPolitics rates 47 Senate seats safe Democratic, 44 safe Republican and nine toss-ups, so the Senate may be tighter than betting markets imply.

The S&P 500 is up roughly 10% on a price basis through November 2, versus the 1.6% gain typically seen by Election Day in a midterm year. Bloomberg data show it is the sixth-best start to a midterm year since 1950.

The VIX was near 19 on November 2, up roughly 25% over the prior month and well below its 52-week high of 35.3. Realized volatility in midterm years has exceeded the prior year's level 80% of the time, rising by an average of 3.5pp.
Chief Economist Arend Kapteyn notes volatility typically falls sharply once results are known, regardless of the outcome.

In midterm years the S&P 500 has typically declined from late August through early October and then rebounded by the following March, with an average return of roughly 14% and a median of 16.4%. The exceptions were 1978, 2002 and 2018. The same-period average in non-midterm years is under 5%.
Justinus Steinhorst notes the S&P 500 has been higher six months after Election Day following every midterm election since 1950.

Strategist Phoebe White sees modest yield-curve flattening pressure in a Democratic sweep, with tight margins and short-lived pressure. A Republican sweep tail scenario could trigger a significant sell-off at the long end because it is not in the price, and it is potentially the most fiscally expansive outcome.

James Kanagasooriam of Focaldata thinks the view that Democrats hold a double-digit generic polling lead may be overstated. He expects Democrats to comfortably take the House but sees the Senate as close to a toss-up, partly because too little attention goes to Democratic-held seats in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire.

UBS lists 10 races to watch on election night, mostly in states with early poll closings: NC-03, PA-01, MI-01, NY-17 and NY-21 in the House, and Ohio, Maine, New Hampshire, Michigan and Kansas in the Senate. NY-17 is flagged as the key House toss-up.

tension_points.bull_case: Betting markets give Democrats 81% odds of Senate control, and the S&P 500 has been higher six months after every midterm since 1950, with volatility typically falling once results are known.
tension_points.bear_case: RealClearPolitics rates nine Senate seats as toss-ups, and Focaldata's Kanagasooriam sees the Senate as close to a toss-up. A Republican sweep tail scenario could cause a long-end sell-off that is not priced.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Early election-night results such as NC-03 (7:30 p.m. ET) and PA-01 (8:00 p.m. ET) showing an unexpectedly close national race.
